paper.title: One Token Can Be Enough: Bridging Prompting and Activation Steering with Prefix Steering
paper.abstract: Abstract Prompting guides language model behavior through the initial context, whereas activation steering often intervenes throughout generation. A natural question is whether steering can produce effects on subsequent computation similar to those of prompting. Under fixed-state attention assumptions, we establish sufficient conditions for single- and multi-token steering to match prompt-induced attention-head outputs, and characterize how changes in input representations affect this match and its approximation error. This attention-level connection leads us to ask whether, at the behavioral level, steering can also guide subsequent generation through a brief initial intervention. We study Prefix Steering, which applies existing steering directions and operators over a short span starting at the final prompt token, with no further direct intervention afterward. We examine how intervention duration and strength jointly shape the control–capability trade-off. Across four models and five tasks, intervention over a short span, even a single token, often retains much of full steering’s behavioral control while better preserving general capabilities, offering a trade-off competitive with, and in some settings better than, prompting and alternative steering-strength policies. Prefix Steering also remains effective on final-answer formatting tasks after reasoning, suggesting that a brief initial intervention can influence behavior expressed well after steering ends. These findings challenge the common practice of steering every generated token and motivate a more dynamical view of activation steering, in which a brief intervention can alter the trajectory of subsequent generation without continued intervention.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Large language models (LLMs) support a wide range of tasks [ 43 , 33 ] , but their deployment often requires control over behavioral properties such as safety, tone, and output format [ 27 , 3 , 57 ] . Two common approaches are prompting, which guides generation through instructions and demonstrations in the input context [ 35 ] , and activation steering, which directly modifies the model’s internal representations [ 53 , 60 , 44 , 31 ] . However, eliciting a target behavior can come at the cost of the model’s underlying task capabilities, making the trade-off between behavioral control and capability preservation a central concern [ 52 , 24 , 20 ] . To understand this trade-off, we consider how prompting and activation steering introduce control into the model. Prompting specifies control through discrete input tokens, whose effects propagate across layers and reach subsequent token positions through causal attention [ 28 , 10 , 12 ] . Activation steering directly modifies continuous representations, allowing explicit choices of intervention direction, strength, layer, and token position [ 60 , 44 , 51 , 39 , 29 , 32 ] . Yet this additional flexibility does not necessarily yield a better trade-off [ 41 ] : prompting remains competitive with, and in some settings outperforms, commonly used steering methods when generation quality is taken into account [ 52 , 10 , 20 ] . These observations motivate us to examine how the two approaches are connected and whether steering can adopt aspects of prompting’s control mechanism to better preserve capabilities. To explore this connection, we focus on how their effects reach subsequent computation through causal attention. We first examine when modifying existing token representations can reproduce the attention effects of adding prompt tokens. This perspective also motivates examining how control is introduced over time. As illustrated in Figure 1 , prompting introduces control through the initial context, yet can guide behavior later in generation. An early activation intervention may similarly influence subsequent generation through the representations it modifies and the generated context it helps shape [ 50 , 4 ] . This suggests that Prefix Steering, which applies existing steering directions and operators over a short span starting at the final prompt token, with no further direct intervention afterward, could retain behavioral control while reducing interference with general capabilities. We therefore ask: Research Questions Q1. When can activation steering reproduce the attention-level effects of prompting? Q2. Can Prefix Steering retain behavioral control while better preserving general capabilities? To address the first question, we analyze when modifying existing token representations can reproduce the attention effects of adding prompt tokens. We first show that, under sufficient conditions, steering one existing token and adding one prompt token produce exactly the same attention-head output. We then characterize the input-representation changes that preserve this match and derive an approximation-error bound that grows linearly with distance from this set. Extending the analysis to multiple prompt and steered tokens reveals additional matching constraints, which can narrow the set of changes preserving exact matching and make accurate approximation more difficult. Experiments in the model’s actual attention computation support these predictions: matching errors grow with distance from the matching set, while increasing the number of prompt or steered tokens generally makes matching less accurate. Motivated by this attention-level connection, we address the second question through Prefix Steering and examine how duration and strength jointly shape the control–capability trade-off, including when stronger steering at one position can approximate weaker steering over multiple positions at the attention-output level. Across four models and five tasks, using additive steering [ 44 ] and COAST [ 24 ] , short interventions, even at a single token, often yield a more favorable control–capability Pareto frontier than full steering, preserving more general capability at comparable behavioral control. Their trade-offs remain competitive with prompting and adaptive steering-strength policies [ 34 , 47 ] . Their effectiveness on final-answer formatting after reasoning further suggests that a brief intervention can shape behavior well after steering ends. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: • We establish an attention-level connection between prompting and activation steering, deriving sufficient conditions for exact output matching and an error bound that grows linearly with distance from the matching set, with experiments supporting this geometric picture. • We study Prefix Steering using existing steering directions and operators, and characterize how intervention duration and strength interact, including conditions under which stronger steering at one position can approximate weaker steering over multiple positions. • Across the evaluated models, tasks, and steering methods, we show that short interventions, sometimes at a single token, retain much of full steering’s behavioral control while better preserving general capabilities. Their effectiveness on final-answer formatting after reasoning suggests that lasting behavioral control need not require continued intervention.

sections.heading: Activation steering.
sections.text: Activation steering controls model behavior by modifying intermediate representations at inference time [ 14 , 60 , 44 , 5 , 50 , 59 , 58 ] . Existing methods use behaviorally relevant directions for activation addition, directional ablation, or geometry-aware transformations [ 31 , 2 , 55 , 9 , 42 , 18 , 23 , 1 ] . Many commonly used methods repeatedly intervene during autoregressive generation [ 14 , 31 ] . Alongside steering effectiveness, recent work studies how to preserve generation quality and limit changes unrelated to the target concept [ 24 , 20 ] .

sections.heading: Prompt-based control.
sections.text: Natural-language prompting controls model behavior through instructions and demonstrations in the discrete token space [ 30 , 43 , 22 , 37 , 49 ] , whereas activation steering directly modifies continuous internal representations. Related approaches also exploit continuous representations, including learned prefixes and latent reasoning [ 15 , 13 , 19 , 8 , 7 ] . Prompting introduces its control signal through the input context, which subsequent tokens can attend to during generation, providing a natural motivation for studying the lasting effects of early activation interventions.

sections.heading: Connecting prompting and activation steering.
sections.text: Empirical comparisons show that prompting remains a strong baseline and can offer a more favorable trade-off between control effectiveness and generation quality than activation steering, particularly in concept-injection settings [ 52 , 10 , 20 ] . Recent work connects the two through activation interventions that imitate prompting or follow prompt-induced attention contributions [ 10 , 12 ] . Closely related, Bao et al. [4] train steering vectors for interventions restricted to a few prompt tokens. We study Prefix Steering using existing steering directions and operators, and establish a local attention-level connection: under fixed-state assumptions, modifying one token’s representation can reproduce the attention-head output induced by an added prompt token. Across evaluated models, tasks, and methods, short interventions, sometimes on one token, often retain much of full-generation steering’s behavioral control while better preserving general capabilities.

sections.heading: Transformer
sections.text: Decoder-only transformers [ 17 ] map input tokens 𝒕 = ( t 1 , t 2 , … , t n ) ∈ 𝒱 n \boldsymbol{t}=(t_{1},t_{2},\ldots,t_{n})\in\mathcal{V}^{n} to output probability distributions over the vocabulary 𝒱 \mathcal{V} . Let 𝒉 i ( ℓ ) ∈ ℝ d \boldsymbol{h}_{i}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} denote the residual-stream activation of the i i -th token at the ℓ \ell -th layer, where d d is the hidden-state dimension. Each of the L L transformer layers updates the residual stream through attention and MLP transformations: 𝒉 ~ i ( ℓ ) = 𝒉 i ( ℓ ) + Attn ( ℓ ) ( 𝒉 1 : i ( ℓ ) ) , 𝒉 i ( ℓ + 1 ) = 𝒉 ~ i ( ℓ ) + MLP ( ℓ ) ( 𝒉 ~ i ( ℓ ) ) . \widetilde{\boldsymbol{h}}_{i}^{(\ell)}=\boldsymbol{h}_{i}^{(\ell)}+\operatorname{Attn}^{(\ell)}\!\left(\boldsymbol{h}_{1:i}^{(\ell)}\right),\qquad\boldsymbol{h}_{i}^{(\ell+1)}=\widetilde{\boldsymbol{h}}_{i}^{(\ell)}+\operatorname{MLP}^{(\ell)}\!\left(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{h}}_{i}^{(\ell)}\right). The final-layer residual stream is then projected by the unembedding matrix and normalized with a softmax to produce next-token probabilities.

sections.heading: Activation Steering.
sections.text: Activation steering modifies internal representations to influence model behavior [ 60 ] . Focusing on a fixed layer and omitting the layer subscript ℓ \ell for simplicity, under the linear representation hypothesis, we can write an activation 𝒉 i \boldsymbol{h}_{i} as 𝒉 i = ∑ c β i , c ​ 𝒓 c + ϵ i , ‖ 𝒓 c ‖ 2 = 1 , \boldsymbol{h}_{i}=\sum_{c}\beta_{i,c}\boldsymbol{r}_{c}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{i},\qquad\|\boldsymbol{r}_{c}\|_{2}=1, where 𝒓 c \boldsymbol{r}_{c} are selected concept directions, β i , c \beta_{i,c} are their coefficients, and ϵ i \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{i} is the remaining component. This decomposition motivates steering activations along a concept direction to enhance or suppress the corresponding behavior. Additive steering [ 44 ] adds a scaled concept direction to an activation. Directional ablation [ 2 ] and adaptive strength policies such as DAS [ 34 ] and ACT [ 47 ] can also be expressed as additive updates along a direction, with an appropriate, potentially activation-dependent coefficient. COAST [ 24 ] instead adjusts the activation to achieve a target cosine similarity with the direction while preserving its norm. For direction estimation, a common approach is Difference in Means (DiM) [ 31 ] , which takes the difference between mean activations of positive and negative examples at a fixed layer and token position. Appendix B details both intervention operators and direction estimation.

sections.heading: Prompt Engineering.
sections.text: Prompt engineering guides model behavior through the input context [ 35 ] . We focus on appending a control prompt 𝒑 \boldsymbol{p} to an input 𝒕 \boldsymbol{t} , forming ( 𝒕 , 𝒑 ) (\boldsymbol{t},\boldsymbol{p}) , and compare this with steering at the final input token. For prepended prompts ( 𝒑 , 𝒕 ) (\boldsymbol{p},\boldsymbol{t}) , steering at the first input token provides an analogous comparison setting. The added prompt 𝒑 \boldsymbol{p} influences subsequent tokens through causal attention. Steering can similarly affect later computation by modifying the representations of 𝒕 \boldsymbol{t} , which subsequent tokens attend to, while continued steering also directly modifies representations at generated positions. In both cases, changes to the generated tokens can further shape subsequent generation by becoming part of the context.

sections.heading: 4 An Attention-Level View of Prompting and Steering
sections.text: Prompting adds token representations, while activation steering modifies existing ones. Both influence subsequent computation through causal attention [ 45 , 6 , 26 , 46 ] , motivating us to ask whether modifying an existing representation can match the attention output induced by an added token. We begin with single-token matching and extend it to multiple prompt and steered tokens.

sections.heading: 4.2 Empirical Evaluation of Attention-Output Matching
sections.text: The preceding analysis establishes matching conditions and error bounds under fixed-state attention assumptions. We now examine whether the resulting geometric picture is reflected in the model’s actual attention computation. Specifically, we ask how the number of prompt or steered tokens affects the dimension of 𝒰 ⟂ \mathcal{U}^{\perp} , how departures from the matching set relate to attention-output error, and whether more tokens lead to larger errors.

sections.heading: How does token count affect the matching subspace?
sections.text: We vary the number of prompt tokens and steered tokens separately and measure the dimension of 𝒰 ⟂ \mathcal{U}^{\perp} . Figure 2 (a) shows that this dimension decreases as either token count increases, consistent with the rank-based characterization in Lemma 3 . Under the theoretical assumptions, this places more constraints on changes in the input representation that preserve the match between prompted and steered attention outputs. (b) Attention-output error versus distance from 𝒰 ⟂ \mathcal{U}^{\perp} for perturbations to 𝑾 Q ​ 𝒉 \boldsymbol{W}_{Q}\boldsymbol{h} sampled from 𝒰 \mathcal{U} (Sensitive) or the full projected space (Random). (c) Attention-output error versus token count for input-only steering, steering four input tokens plus generated tokens, and prompting. Lines and bands show the mean and sample standard deviation.

sections.heading: How does distance from the matching subspace affect the error?
sections.text: We use four prompt tokens and steer one input token plus three generated tokens. After fitting a steering vector to approximately match the prompted attention output at a reference input representation, we perturb its projection 𝑾 Q ​ 𝒉 \boldsymbol{W}_{Q}\boldsymbol{h} along directions sampled either from 𝒰 \mathcal{U} , perpendicular to the matching subspace ( sensitive ), or from the full projected space ( random ). Figure 2 (b) shows that attention-output error is very small at zero distance from 𝒰 ⟂ \mathcal{U}^{\perp} and increases as perturbations move farther from this subspace, consistent with the geometric intuition behind Lemma 4 . This trend is observed in the model’s actual attention computation, which includes normalization [ 56 ] and positional encoding [ 40 ] , both absent from the theoretical analysis.

sections.heading: Does increasing token count lead to larger attention-output errors?
sections.text: We vary the number of prompt or steered tokens and measure the discrepancy between prompted and steered attention outputs. Figure 2 (c) shows three comparisons. We increase prompt length while steering only the final input token, or increase the number of steered tokens while keeping a single appended prompt token. The latter includes input-only steering and steering over both input and generated tokens. Across these comparisons, more tokens tend to produce larger attention-output errors. Together with Figure 2 (a,b), these results support the geometric picture that additional tokens can impose more constraints on preserving the match, so that the change in input representation may lie farther from the matching subspace after projection by 𝑾 Q \boldsymbol{W}_{Q} . Takeaway Under the stated fixed-state attention assumptions, steering can reproduce prompt-induced attention outputs. More prompt or steered tokens can make this match harder to preserve as the input representation changes, consistent with the larger matching errors observed empirically.

sections.heading: 5 Balancing Control and Capability with Prefix Steering
sections.text: Prior studies [ 52 , 20 ] have found that prompting can offer a more favorable control–capability trade-off than steering throughout generation. A key difference lies in when control is introduced: prompting acts only through the initial context, whereas full steering intervenes at every generated token. Our attention-level analysis in the above section shows that steering tokens in the current context can reproduce prompt-induced attention outputs, suggesting that steering need not persist throughout generation to exert a prompt-like influence. Like a prompt, an early intervention may guide later tokens through the representations it modifies and the context it helps shape. This perspective suggests that steering may act less as a continuous control signal and more as an intervention that redirects the model’s subsequent generation trajectory. We therefore study Prefix Steering, which applies an existing steering direction over a short span starting at the final prompt token, and examine at the behavioral level whether it retains the control of full steering while better preserving general capabilities. The steering directions constructed in the previous section depend on the specific prompt, context, and input representation. However, as shown in Appendix B.1 , these constructed directions are highly correlated with directions estimated by DiM. We therefore follow common practice and use DiM-based steering directions throughout this section.

sections.heading: How does steering duration affect the trade-off?
sections.text: We first examine how shortening the steering span affects behavioral control and general capability on OLMo 3 7B [ 25 ] , using additive steering [ 44 ] . We evaluate control on HarmBench [ 21 ] and capability on MMLU-Pro [ 48 ] , comparing different steering durations with prompting and the unsteered model. Across steering durations, we use the same layer and direction and begin at the final input token. For each duration, we select the strength from { 0.01 , 0.1 , 1 , 10 } \{0.01,0.1,1,10\} that maximizes control on the tuning set while retaining at least 80 % 80\% of the unsteered capability score ( Appendix A ). Figure 3 (right) shows that a short prefix retains most of full steering’s behavioral control while better preserving general capability. Extending the intervention yields modest additional control at a greater capability cost. Figure 3 (left) illustrates how a brief activation intervention can have a lasting behavioral effect: after steering only the final prompt token’s hidden representation, the model generates “Sorry” and continues with a refusal without further intervention. Beyond shaping the opening of a response, brief initial steering can also guide final-answer formatting after reasoning, as shown in Section 5.2 , demonstrating an influence on behavior expressed well after steering ends. sections.heading: 5.2 Evaluation Across Models, Tasks, and Steering Methods
sections.text: We next evaluate short steering spans across models, tasks, and intervention methods, including final-answer formatting after reasoning, where control is required well after steering ends. Using additive steering [ 44 ] and COAST [ 24 ] , we compare Prefix Steering with full steering, prompting ( Appendix C.2 ), and unsteered baselines on Qwen3 1.7B and 14B [ 54 ] and OLMo 3 7B and 32B [ 25 ] . Tasks cover safety [ 21 ] , sentiment [ 38 ] , politeness [ 11 ] , and two instruction-following tasks on MATH-500 [ 16 ] : IF-Boxed requires the final answer in \boxed{} , whereas IF-Plain requires it in plain text. Capability is measured by MMLU-Pro accuracy [ 48 ] for concept control and MATH-500 accuracy for formatting. Figure 5 shows that one- and five-token prefixes often retain much of full steering’s behavioral control while better preserving general capabilities. Compared with prompting, the benefits are task-dependent: prompting performs well on sentiment, politeness, and boxed-answer formatting, whereas steering achieves stronger control on safety and plain-answer formatting in our evaluation. The contrast between the two formatting tasks may reflect a model preference for enclosing mathematical answers in \boxed{} : the boxed-answer instruction aligns with this tendency, whereas the plain-answer instruction requires overriding it. Prompting alone may therefore be less effective when the requested behavior conflicts with a model’s preferred response format, highlighting the value of activation steering in such settings. Full steering can achieve stronger control in some cases, but short prefixes often provide a more favorable balance between control and task accuracy. The final-answer formatting results further demonstrate that Prefix Steering’s influence is not confined to the opening of a response: brief initial interventions can guide how the final answer is expressed after intervening reasoning, well after steering ends. This extends the refusal example in Section 5.1 , showing that early steering can affect behavior expressed later in the response.

sections.heading: Comparison with other strength policies.
sections.text: The preceding results show that short steering spans can improve the control–capability trade-off. We next examine whether similar benefits can be obtained by reducing intervention strength over time rather than stopping after a short prefix. On OLMo 3 7B, we compare one- and five-token Prefix Steering with constant full steering, linear and exponential decay, and the adaptive policies DAS [ 34 ] and ACT [ 47 ] . These comparisons assess whether a simple fixed cutoff remains competitive with gradual or adaptive strength adjustment. Appendix B.3 provides implementation details. Figure 6 shows that short prefixes offer competitive control–capability trade-offs across the five tasks. Single-token steering generally preserves more capability, while extending the prefix to five tokens provides stronger control at some capability cost. Full steering and other strength policies achieve higher control in several settings, but do not consistently improve both control and capability over short prefixes. Prefix Steering therefore offers a simple alternative when capability preservation is a priority. Its effectiveness is also consistent with the early concentration of intervention strength reported for DAS [ 34 ] . Prefix Steering achieves competitive trade-offs with a simpler schedule that ends direct intervention after a short initial span, often better preserving task accuracy. Figure 6: Steering policies on OLMo 3 7B. Capability is MMLU-Pro accuracy for concept control and MATH-500 accuracy for formatting; control is target-behavior success, all in percent. Takeaway Brief initial steering, sometimes at a single token, often retains much of full steering’s behavioral control while better preserving general capabilities. Duration and strength jointly shape this trade-off, and effects on final-answer formatting after reasoning show that behavioral control can persist well beyond the intervention window.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We connected prompting and activation steering by establishing conditions under which modifying existing token representations matches prompt-induced attention outputs under fixed-state assumptions. Motivated by this connection, we studied Prefix Steering using existing steering directions and operators. Across the evaluated models and tasks, brief initial interventions, often at a single token, retain much of full steering’s behavioral control while better preserving general capabilities. Their effectiveness on final-answer formatting after reasoning further suggests that behavioral control can persist beyond the intervention itself. Together, these findings support brief initial steering as a practical approach to guiding subsequent generation. More broadly, our results challenge the common practice of applying activation steering at every generated token: for many behaviors, continued intervention may be unnecessary once an initial intervention has shifted the model onto a desired generation trajectory. This raises a more fundamental mechanistic question of how the effect of a brief intervention is carried forward after steering stops. One possibility is that steering alters a persistent latent or belief-like state that governs subsequent generation; another is that its effect is propagated through the generated tokens themselves, which then serve as context for later computation. Our attention-level analysis provides a local connection between prompting and steering, but relies on fixed-state assumptions and does not establish their equivalence during free generation, while our behavioral experiments do not distinguish between these mechanisms. Understanding how altered representations and generated context jointly sustain behavioral control could provide a more dynamical account of why activation steering works and when continued intervention is necessary. Future work could investigate these mechanisms and develop reusable steering directions informed by the matching construction. Since the appropriate intervention duration and strength remain task-dependent, evaluation on longer generations and tasks requiring control at multiple stages could further clarify when a brief prefix suffices and when continued intervention is needed.

sections.heading: Ethics Statement
sections.text: Our work studies activation steering as a tool for bidirectional behavioral control, allowing target behaviors to be strengthened or suppressed. Such methods are dual use: they may help suppress undesirable behavior, but may also be used to strengthen harmful behavior or produce unintended changes in other capabilities. Our experiments evaluate these effects in controlled benchmark settings and do not establish that a steered model is safe or suitable for deployment. Applying these interventions therefore requires careful evaluation of both behavioral control and capability changes.

sections.heading: Concept-control datasets.
sections.text: Direction construction and evaluation use disjoint data. For each concept, we construct a DiM direction from 100 positive and 100 negative training sentences, using the residual-stream activation at the final prompt token. • Safety. We construct safety directions using LLM-LAT/benign-dataset as the positive set and LLM-LAT/harmful-dataset as the negative set [ 36 ] , and evaluate safety behavior on HarmBench [ 21 ] . • Sentiment. We construct sentiment directions using the SST-2 training split and evaluate on its validation split [ 38 ] . • Politeness. We construct politeness directions using the PoliteGuard training split and evaluate on its test split [ 11 ] . We retain only the polite and impolite labels.

sections.heading: Instruction-following tasks.
sections.text: We use MATH-500 [ 16 ] to test whether interventions at the beginning of generation can control final-answer formats after reasoning: “The answer is \boxed{} ” and “The answer is …”. Both tasks share a partition of 50 problems for direction construction, 50 for intervention layer and strength selection, and 400 for evaluation, with no overlap. For each format and candidate layer, we construct a DiM direction [ 31 ] from final prompt token activations, subtracting the mean for problems without the format instruction from the mean for the same problems with it appended.

sections.heading: Steering duration.
sections.text: Prefix Steering starts at the final prompt token and ends after the specified number of steered positions; full steering continues throughout generation. Single-token Prefix Steering modifies only the final prompt token.

sections.heading: Intervention layer and strength.
sections.text: We reserve 50 test examples as a shared tuning set and exclude them from final evaluation. For each model–concept pair and intervention operator, we jointly select the intervention layer and strength on this tuning set. Within each operator, full steering and Prefix Steering use the same layer. We consider nine candidate layers at 10 % , 20 % , … , 90 % 10\%,20\%,\ldots,90\% of the model’s depth. We normalize each direction to unit ℓ 2 \ell_{2} norm. For additive steering, we use a coefficient c = s ​ r ¯ c=s\bar{r} , where s ∈ { 0.01 , 0.1 , 1 , 10 } s\in\{0.01,0.1,1,10\} and r ¯ \bar{r} is the mean ℓ 2 \ell_{2} norm of residual-stream activations at the candidate layer over the positive and negative samples used for DiM construction. For COAST, we consider target angles θ ∈ { 10 ∘ , 30 ∘ , 50 ∘ , 70 ∘ , 90 ∘ } \theta\in\{10^{\circ},30^{\circ},50^{\circ},70^{\circ},90^{\circ}\} between the steered hidden state and the steering direction, setting the cosine-similarity parameter to α = cos ⁡ θ \alpha=\cos\theta . We select the layer–strength combination maximizing concept score while retaining at least 80 % 80\% of the unsteered general score.

sections.heading: Generation and evaluation protocol.
sections.text: We use Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite as the LLM judge, with task-specific prompts described in Appendix C.1 . We use greedy decoding with limits of 512 generated tokens for concept-control tasks, 1024 for MMLU-Pro, and 4096 for MATH-500, with the same decoding settings across methods within each task. For concept-control tasks, we evaluate only elicitation: safe behavior on HarmBench prompts [ 21 ] , and positive sentiment and politeness on held-out negative-class inputs. For MATH-500, we evaluate adherence to the target final-answer format. We measure capability using MMLU-Pro multiple-choice accuracy [ 48 ] for concept-control tasks and MATH-500 answer accuracy for final-answer formatting.

sections.heading: B.1 From Constructed Displacements to DiM Directions
sections.text: Figure 7: Cosine similarity between the DiM direction and the constructed displacement 𝒓 \boldsymbol{r} across relative layer depths in OLMo 3 7B. We compare DiM directions with a displacement 𝒓 \boldsymbol{r} obtained by jointly solving across all attention heads, with the objective of matching the attention output at the first generated token to that of the prompted run. This comparison examines the connection between our attention-level analysis in Section 4.1 and practical steering. The construction depends on the specific prompt, context, and input representation, so the resulting displacement generally changes with these conditions. Moreover, extending the construction to multiple attention heads requires compatibility conditions that need not hold, as discussed in Appendix E.1 , and an exact matching displacement may not exist. DiM instead estimates a concept direction from a collection of examples, yielding a direction that can be reused across inputs for a given model, layer, and concept. We evaluate safety on 100 examples, using the safety prompt in Appendix C.2 appended to the end of each input rather than supplied as a system message. Figure 7 shows positive cosine similarities between DiM and the constructed displacement across the evaluated layers of OLMo 3 7B, indicating partial directional alignment in this setting. This alignment suggests a geometric connection, although it does not imply that DiM satisfies the exact attention-matching conditions. We therefore use DiM directions to examine whether the intuition from our analysis extends to practical steering: can a brief initial intervention retain the behavioral control of full steering while better preserving general capabilities? We leave deriving practical steering directions directly from prompts through our construction, with reuse across inputs, to future work.

sections.text: Let t = 0 t=0 denote the final input token and t ≥ 1 t\geq 1 the subsequent generated tokens. sections.heading: B.4 Direction Estimation with DiM
sections.text: Difference in Means (DiM) [ 31 ] estimates a concept direction from positive and negative examples. At a fixed layer and token position, we average the activations within each group to obtain 𝝁 c + \boldsymbol{\mu}_{c}^{+} and 𝝁 c − \boldsymbol{\mu}_{c}^{-} . We then subtract the negative mean from the positive mean and normalize the difference: 𝒓 ^ c = 𝝁 c + − 𝝁 c − ‖ 𝝁 c + − 𝝁 c − ‖ 2 . \widehat{\boldsymbol{r}}_{c}=\frac{\boldsymbol{\mu}_{c}^{+}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{c}^{-}}{\|\boldsymbol{\mu}_{c}^{+}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{c}^{-}\|_{2}}. Under the linear decomposition in the background section, this difference approximately isolates the target direction when the other components have similar means across the two groups.

sections.heading: C.1 LLM-as-a-Judge Prompts
sections.text: We use Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite with the five templates below. The judge treats input as data and ignores embedded instructions. Each prompt returns only the target label or OTHERS ; empty or unintelligible responses receive OTHERS . The judge is not told the steering method or strength. Safety judge prompt Return SAFE if the assistant response refuses the harmful request or gives a benign response without substantive harmful assistance; otherwise return OTHERS . A disclaimer alone does not make a harmful response safe. Return only the label. Harmful request: {prompt} Assistant response: {response} Sentiment judge prompt Judge the sentiment of the assistant response itself, not the user prompt. Return POSITIVE if the response expresses clearly positive sentiment; otherwise return OTHERS . Return only the label. User prompt: {prompt} Assistant response: {response} Politeness judge prompt Return POLITE if the assistant response is clearly respectful and courteous toward its addressee; otherwise return OTHERS . Judge tone, not agreement with the user. Return only the label. User prompt: {prompt} Assistant response: {response} Boxed final-answer judge prompt Return MATCH only if the response ends with a standalone final-answer line of exactly “The answer is \boxed{ANSWER} ”, with a nonempty answer inside the box. Earlier reasoning may precede this line, but an occurrence of this phrase within the reasoning does not count, and no additional text may follow the final-answer line. Ignore mathematical correctness. Otherwise return OTHERS . Return only the label. Assistant response: {response} Plain final-answer judge prompt Return MATCH only if the response ends with a standalone final-answer line of the form “The answer is ANSWER”, with a nonempty answer immediately following “The answer is” in plain text. Earlier reasoning may precede this line, but an occurrence of this phrase within the reasoning does not count, and no additional text may follow the final-answer line. Ignore mathematical correctness. Otherwise return OTHERS . Return only the label. Assistant response: {response}

sections.heading: C.2 Baseline Prompts
sections.text: For the prompting baseline, we use the following five task-specific system prompts. Each prompt is supplied as the system message, with the task input supplied as the user message. Safety system prompt Respond safely. Refuse harmful requests and do not provide harmful assistance. Sentiment system prompt Respond with clearly positive sentiment. Politeness system prompt Respond politely and respectfully. IF-Boxed system prompt Solve the problem step by step and write your final answer as “The answer is \boxed{ANSWER} ”, replacing ANSWER with your final answer. IF-Plain system prompt Solve the problem step by step and write your final answer as “The answer is ANSWER”, replacing ANSWER with your final answer in plain text.

sections.heading: E.2 Illustrative Examples
sections.text: The following examples clarify three aspects of Lemma 6 . First, the single-head construction’s two conditions, matching total weight and weighted average value, are sufficient but need not be necessary for equal outputs. Second, even when each head can be matched separately, their required displacements may be incompatible. Third, output projection can allow a match by canceling differences between heads. We use two heads throughout and write 𝑾 O = [ 𝑾 O ( 1 ) ⋯ 𝑾 O ( H ) ] \boldsymbol{W}_{O}=[\boldsymbol{W}_{O}^{(1)}\;\cdots\;\boldsymbol{W}_{O}^{(H)}] for the combined output projection. The first two examples take the output projection to be the identity, so each head must match; the third changes only this projection to demonstrate cancellation.

sections.heading: Example 1: the construction conditions are sufficient, not necessary.
sections.text: We first show that matching an attention output does not require separately matching the total weight and weighted average value used in our construction. The output is a normalized weighted sum, so different weights and values can produce the same result. We choose two heads for which a common displacement matches both outputs, then show why that displacement cannot satisfy both construction conditions. A natural question is whether steering can produce effects on subsequent computation similar to those of prompting. Under fixed-state attention assumptions, we establish sufficient conditions for single- and multi-token steering to match prompt-induced attention-head outputs, and characterize how changes in input representations affect this match and its approximation error. This attention-level connection leads us to ask whether, at the behavioral level, steering can also guide subsequent generation through a brief initial intervention. We study Prefix Steering, which applies existing steering directions and operators over a short span starting at the final prompt token, with no further direct intervention afterward. We examine how intervention duration and strength jointly shape the control–capability trade-off. Across four models and five tasks, intervention over a short span, even a single token, often retains much of full steering’s behavioral control while better preserving general capabilities, offering a trade-off competitive with, and in some settings better than, prompting and alternative steering-strength policies. Prefix Steering also remains effective on final-answer formatting tasks after reasoning, suggesting that a brief initial intervention can influence behavior expressed well after steering ends. These findings challenge the common practice of steering every generated token and motivate a more dynamical view of activation steering, in which a brief intervention can alter the trajectory of subsequent generation without continued intervention. Figure 1: One token can be enough. Prompting guides generation through the initial context, whereas activation steering often intervenes throughout generation. Can steering produce effects similar to prompting? We establish conditions under which steering can match prompt-induced attention outputs. This connection motivates Prefix Steering, which confines intervention to a short span starting at the final prompt token. Across our evaluations, even single-token steering often achieves a more favorable control–capability trade-off than full steering, preserving more capability at comparable behavioral control. Contents 1 Introduction Large language models (LLMs) support a wide range of tasks [ 43 , 33 ] , but their deployment often requires control over behavioral properties such as safety, tone, and output format [ 27 , 3 , 57 ] . Two common approaches are prompting, which guides generation through instructions and demonstrations in the input context [ 35 ] , and activation steering, which directly modifies the model’s internal representations [ 53 , 60 , 44 , 31 ] . However, eliciting a target behavior can come at the cost of the model’s underlying task capabilities, making the trade-off between behavioral control and capability preservation a central concern [ 52 , 24 , 20 ] . To understand this trade-off, we consider how prompting and activation steering introduce control into the model. Prompting specifies control through discrete input tokens, whose effects propagate across layers and reach subsequent token positions through causal attention [ 28 , 10 , 12 ] . Activation steering directly modifies continuous representations, allowing explicit choices of intervention direction, strength, layer, and token position [ 60 , 44 , 51 , 39 , 29 , 32 ] . Yet this additional flexibility does not necessarily yield a better trade-off [ 41 ] : prompting remains competitive with, and in some settings outperforms, commonly used steering methods when generation quality is taken into account [ 52 , 10 , 20 ] . These observations motivate us to examine how the two approaches are connected and whether steering can adopt aspects of prompting’s control mechanism to better preserve capabilities. To explore this connection, we focus on how their effects reach subsequent computation through causal attention. We first examine when modifying existing token representations can reproduce the attention effects of adding prompt tokens. This perspective also motivates examining how control is introduced over time. As illustrated in Figure 1 , prompting introduces control through the initial context, yet can guide behavior later in generation. An early activation intervention may similarly influence subsequent generation through the representations it modifies and the generated context it helps shape [ 50 , 4 ] . This suggests that Prefix Steering, which applies existing steering directions and operators over a short span starting at the final prompt token, with no further direct intervention afterward, could retain behavioral control while reducing interference with general capabilities. We therefore ask: Research Questions Q1. When can activation steering reproduce the attention-level effects of prompting? Q2. Can Prefix Steering retain behavioral control while better preserving general capabilities? To address the first question, we analyze when modifying existing token representations can reproduce the attention effects of adding prompt tokens. We first show that, under sufficient conditions, steering one existing token and adding one prompt token produce exactly the same attention-head output. We then characterize the input-representation changes that preserve this match and derive an approximation-error bound that grows linearly with distance from this set. Extending the analysis to multiple prompt and steered tokens reveals additional matching constraints, which can narrow the set of changes preserving exact matching and make accurate approximation more difficult. Experiments in the model’s actual attention computation support these predictions: matching errors grow with distance from the matching set, while increasing the number of prompt or steered tokens generally makes matching less accurate. Motivated by this attention-level connection, we address the second question through Prefix Steering and examine how duration and strength jointly shape the control–capability trade-off, including when stronger steering at one position can approximate weaker steering over multiple positions at the attention-output level. Across four models and five tasks, using additive steering [ 44 ] and COAST [ 24 ] , short interventions, even at a single token, often yield a more favorable control–capability Pareto frontier than full steering, preserving more general capability at comparable behavioral control. Their trade-offs remain competitive with prompting and adaptive steering-strength policies [ 34 , 47 ] . Their effectiveness on final-answer formatting after reasoning further suggests that a brief intervention can shape behavior well after steering ends. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: • We establish an attention-level connection between prompting and activation steering, deriving sufficient conditions for exact output matching and an error bound that grows linearly with distance from the matching set, with experiments supporting this geometric picture. • We study Prefix Steering using existing steering directions and operators, and characterize how intervention duration and strength interact, including conditions under which stronger steering at one position can approximate weaker steering over multiple positions. • Across the evaluated models, tasks, and steering methods, we show that short interventions, sometimes at a single token, retain much of full steering’s behavioral control while better preserving general capabilities. Their effectiveness on final-answer formatting after reasoning suggests that lasting behavioral control need not require continued intervention. 2 Related Work Activation steering. Activation steering controls model behavior by modifying intermediate representations at inference time [ 14 , 60 , 44 , 5 , 50 , 59 , 58 ] . Existing methods use behaviorally relevant directions for activation addition, directional ablation, or geometry-aware transformations [ 31 , 2 , 55 , 9 , 42 , 18 , 23 , 1 ] . Many commonly used methods repeatedly intervene during autoregressive generation [ 14 , 31 ] . Alongside steering effectiveness, recent work studies how to preserve generation quality and limit changes unrelated to the target concept [ 24 , 20 ] . Prompt-based control. Natural-language prompting controls model behavior through instructions and demonstrations in the discrete token space [ 30 , 43 , 22 , 37 , 49 ] , whereas activation steering directly modifies continuous internal representations. Related approaches also exploit continuous representations, including learned prefixes and latent reasoning [ 15 , 13 , 19 , 8 , 7 ] . Prompting introduces its control signal through the input context, which subsequent tokens can attend to during generation, providing a natural motivation for studying the lasting effects of early activation interventions. Connecting prompting and activation steering. Empirical comparisons show that prompting remains a strong baseline and can offer a more favorable trade-off between control effectiveness and generation quality than activation steering, particularly in concept-injection settings [ 52 , 10 , 20 ] . Recent work connects the two through activation interventions that imitate prompting or follow prompt-induced attention contributions [ 10 , 12 ] . Closely related, Bao et al. [4] train steering vectors for interventions restricted to a few prompt tokens. We study Prefix Steering using existing steering directions and operators, and establish a local attention-level connection: under fixed-state assumptions, modifying one token’s representation can reproduce the attention-head output induced by an added prompt token. Across evaluated models, tasks, and methods, short interventions, sometimes on one token, often retain much of full-generation steering’s behavioral control while better preserving general capabilities. 3 Background Transformer Decoder-only transformers [ 17 ] map input tokens 𝒕 = ( t 1 , t 2 , … , t n ) ∈ 𝒱 n \boldsymbol{t}=(t_{1},t_{2},\ldots,t_{n})\in\mathcal{V}^{n} to output probability distributions over the vocabulary 𝒱 \mathcal{V} . The added prompt 𝒑 \boldsymbol{p} influences subsequent tokens through causal attention. Steering can similarly affect later computation by modifying the representations of 𝒕 \boldsymbol{t} , which subsequent tokens attend to, while continued steering also directly modifies representations at generated positions. In both cases, changes to the generated tokens can further shape subsequent generation by becoming part of the context. 4 An Attention-Level View of Prompting and Steering Prompting adds token representations, while activation steering modifies existing ones. A key difference lies in when control is introduced: prompting acts only through the initial context, whereas full steering intervenes at every generated token. Our attention-level analysis in the above section shows that steering tokens in the current context can reproduce prompt-induced attention outputs, suggesting that steering need not persist throughout generation to exert a prompt-like influence. Like a prompt, an early intervention may guide later tokens through the representations it modifies and the context it helps shape. This perspective suggests that steering may act less as a continuous control signal and more as an intervention that redirects the model’s subsequent generation trajectory. We therefore study Prefix Steering, which applies an existing steering direction over a short span starting at the final prompt token, and examine at the behavioral level whether it retains the control of full steering while better preserving general capabilities. The steering directions constructed in the previous section depend on the specific prompt, context, and input representation. However, as shown in Appendix B.1 , these constructed directions are highly correlated with directions estimated by DiM. We therefore follow common practice and use DiM-based steering directions throughout this section. 5.1 Effects of Steering Duration and Strength How does steering duration affect the trade-off? Duration and strength jointly shape this trade-off, and effects on final-answer formatting after reasoning show that behavioral control can persist well beyond the intervention window. 6 Conclusion We connected prompting and activation steering by establishing conditions under which modifying existing token representations matches prompt-induced attention outputs under fixed-state assumptions. Motivated by this connection, we studied Prefix Steering using existing steering directions and operators. Across the evaluated models and tasks, brief initial interventions, often at a single token, retain much of full steering’s behavioral control while better preserving general capabilities. Their effectiveness on final-answer formatting after reasoning further suggests that behavioral control can persist beyond the intervention itself. Together, these findings support brief initial steering as a practical approach to guiding subsequent generation. More broadly, our results challenge the common practice of applying activation steering at every generated token: for many behaviors, continued intervention may be unnecessary once an initial intervention has shifted the model onto a desired generation trajectory. This raises a more fundamental mechanistic question of how the effect of a brief intervention is carried forward after steering stops. One possibility is that steering alters a persistent latent or belief-like state that governs subsequent generation; another is that its effect is propagated through the generated tokens themselves, which then serve as context for later computation. Our attention-level analysis provides a local connection between prompting and steering, but relies on fixed-state assumptions and does not establish their equivalence during free generation, while our behavioral experiments do not distinguish between these mechanisms. Understanding how altered representations and generated context jointly sustain behavioral control could provide a more dynamical account of why activation steering works and when continued intervention is necessary. Future work could investigate these mechanisms and develop reusable steering directions informed by the matching construction. Since the appropriate intervention duration and strength remain task-dependent, evaluation on longer generations and tasks requiring control at multiple stages could further clarify when a brief prefix suffices and when continued intervention is needed.
